_about: The suite's vocabulary. Prompts, the website and the docs use these terms as defined here, and avoid the listed alternatives (tests check). GLOSSARY.md and the website's help are generated from this file; `gradekit glossary TERM` looks one up.

terms.definition: One of the 35 things the suite grades, such as A2 Security & Privacy. Each has a rubric with what to assess and what each score means.
A group of benchmarks (A to F, plus X for the conditional ones). A pillar's score is the weighted average of its benchmarks.
A whole number from 1 to 10 for a benchmark, set by the grader from evidence. The overall score and pillar scores are weighted averages computed by gradekit.
Whether a benchmark applies to a project: full, limited (counts at most weight 1 and its target is capped) or not applicable (weight 0, no score). Decided by the project's purpose, never its quality.
How much a benchmark counts, from 1 to 3 (0 when not applicable). It starts from the base weight and is moved by the project's answers and overrides.
A starting set of answers for a kind of project, such as service, library or prototype.
A project's replies to the eight questions in `project.toml` (sensitive data, users, lifespan…). Each answer moves specific weights and may make a benchmark a gate.
A short hash of everything in the effective config that affects scores. Reports with different fingerprints were weighted differently.
A non-negotiable benchmark. A gate at or below the hard floor (3 by default) caps the overall score (at 4.0 by default), and every gate must reach a minimum for each maturity level.
Where the code stands, from L0 (not viable) to L4 (exemplary), set by fixed requirements on gates, pillars and the overall score.
The score a benchmark should reach, from its weight (proportional targets: 10, 9 or 8). The improver stops at each benchmark's target.
Everything gradekit computes from a report's scores: pillar and overall scores, gates, maturity, targets, zones and ranked priorities. Never computed by hand.
A specific problem in the code, with an ID (A3-002), a severity, a status and evidence. Findings keep their ID from one report to the next.
A problem first recorded in this report that was already there before: the previous report missed it. It counts as open, but a PR check never fails because of it.
How bad a finding is: critical, major or minor, as the grader judged it.
A finding's severity after its zone: one level higher in a hot zone, one lower in a cold zone (never lower for security findings). It decides priorities.
A part of the code marked hot (problems there count more: money, access, important data), normal, or cold (count less: scripts, examples). The first matching zone wins.
What a claim rests on: a code citation (file, lines and exact quote), a command and its output, or an absence (what was searched for and how).
Code evidence: a file, line range and the exact quote. gradekit checks every citation against the code.
Positive evidence for a benchmark. A score of 9 needs at least one.
Evidence that a benchmark's quality is kept up automatically (a CI job, a lint rule, a test). A score of 10 needs it.
A finding people decided to leave as it is (for example, won't fix by design). It's listed in `dispositions.json` and stops lowering scores.
A finding whose details would help an attacker. Its details are withheld from the public report and kept in `report.private.json`.
Tests kept out of the graded repo and run against it, to catch a grade that doesn't match behaviour. Off unless you turn them on.
Text in the graded repo that tries to influence the grader. It caps maturity at L1 for that report.
A sign that code was written to look good to the grader rather than to work better, such as tests that assert nothing.
One step on a benchmark's path to its target, with the findings it resolves, the expected new score and the effort.
An action's place in the ranked list gradekit makes from tiers, zones and expected gain.
A priority group: fix first (tier 0: a failed gate, or a critical finding in a hot zone), unblocks the next maturity level (1), below target (2), optional (3).
A yes-or-no question a person must answer before an action is done, because it changes behaviour, scope or a public interface.
The answer to a decision question, kept in `decisions.json`. Append-only: the newest answer wins.
The repo that holds every project's grading files: `projects/NAME/` with `project.toml`, `decisions.json`, `dispositions.json` and `reports/`. Separate from the code it grades.
One graded codebase (or part of a monorepo), with its own folder in the grading repo.
One grading of one commit: `report.json` (the data) and `report.md` (made from it), in `reports/<date>-<commit>/`. Never edited after it's committed.
The report that is committed when sensitive findings are withheld. The full report is `report.private.json`, which is never committed.
`projects/index.json`: every project's latest score, maturity, history and decisions waiting, made by `gradekit index`.
The agent that grades the code (`prompts/grader.md`). It never changes the code.
The agent that checks a grader's report and prepares the decision questions (`prompts/reviewer.md`). People can use the Review page instead.
The agent that works down a report's priorities and stops at each benchmark's target (`prompts/improver.md`).
The agent that runs a PR check (`prompts/pr-review.md`).
A quick re-grade of only what a pull request touches, against the last report. It passes or fails: any score that drops fails it. On GitLab, the same for a merge request.
A benchmark copied unchanged from the last report in a PR check, because the change doesn't touch it.
Something that got worse: a score that dropped, a finding that came back, or a new critical finding.
The improver's before-and-after record of the code's own checks (tests, linters, type checker, build) and of its suppressions and skipped tests. `guard compare` fails if any got worse.
The report made from three independent graders: the median score of each benchmark, with the ones they disagree on flagged.
How an agent hands back its work: a pull request, files saved in a folder, or the chat.
